title: Inside the Delhi Home Holding Indoor AQI at 10-15 With 15,000 Plants
excerpt: As Delhi's air stayed in the very poor range under GRAP Stage III, Peter Singh and Neeno Kaur's Sainik Farms home — built around 15,000 plants, filtered air and aquaponics — is drawing attention again for indoor readings of 10-15.
body:
• Peter Singh, 81, and Neeno Kaur, 72, maintain indoor air quality readings of around 10-15 at their Sainik Farms home in South Delhi, Mint reported, while Delhi recorded an AQI of 321 at 7 a.m. on Thursday.
  • The system is built on about 15,000 plants, filtered air and aquaponics: four large fish tanks whose nutrient-rich water circulates to plants that absorb the nutrients and help filter the water before it returns.
  • The couple grow most of their own food in the setup, which they built after Neeno's cancer diagnosis; she has been cancer-free since 2010, The Better India reported.
  • Context for readers in Delhi: GRAP Stage III restrictions remain in force across NCR, imposed on November 6 after the daily average AQI reached 382 — the couple's home is a long-built exception, not a quick fix for this week's air.

One house in South Delhi is breathing different air from the rest of the capital. Peter Satwant Singh, 81, and his wife Neeno Kaur, 72, maintain an indoor air quality index of around 10-15 at their home in Sainik Farms, according to Mint's report — on a Thursday when Delhi recorded an AQI of 321 at 7 a.m., in the very poor category, according to Central Pollution Control Board data cited by ANI.

How the house works

The home is built as a green ecosystem rather than a sealed box with purifiers. Around 15,000 plants form a major part of it, alongside air filtration. Its engine is aquaponics — a method combining fish farming with soilless plant growing. The setup includes four large aquariums; nutrient-containing water from the tanks circulates to the plants, which absorb the nutrients and help filter the water before it returns to the tanks. The couple grow most of their own food this way.

The Better India, which profiled the home in 2024 when it was recording an AQI of around 15, reported that the plants are grown without soil or chemical fertilisers, and that the house stays at about 25 degrees Celsius even in Delhi's peak summer heat.

Why they built it

The couple's turn to this way of living began with a health crisis: Neeno's cancer diagnosis. Determined to embrace a healthier lifestyle, they turned to aquaponics, The Better India reported; Neeno has been cancer-free since 2010. The home has come back into focus this week because the contrast around it has sharpened — the Commission for Air Quality Management put GRAP Stage III restrictions in force across the National Capital Region on November 6, after the daily average AQI reached 382.

What a reader can take from it

The honest limit is scale: this is a house and grounds rebuilt over years around plants, water and filtration, not a product a family can install during a smog week. What it demonstrates is the size of the gap — indoor readings of 10-15 against a city at 321 — and that the gap was closed with a living system maintained daily, not a single device. For everyone else in Delhi this week, the operative facts remain the city's: GRAP Stage III is in force, and outdoor AQI, not a showcase home, is what governs school, work and travel decisions.
